skills.title: OO design
skills.summary: SOLID, DRY and KISS applied to classes and modules

concepts.title: Single responsibility principle
concepts.summary: A module should have one reason to change: one owner, one kind of rule

variants.q: An `InvoiceService` class calculates tax, renders the invoice PDF and emails it. Switching email providers means editing and redeploying the same class that holds the tax rules. Which principle is this design breaking?
choices: Single responsibility principle
Liskov substitution principle
Interface segregation principle
Open/closed principle
variants.explain: Tax rules, PDF layout and email delivery change for different reasons, often requested by different people, so they belong in separate modules. Open/closed is about extending behaviour without editing existing code, which isn't the core problem here.

variants.q: A `User` model has `save()`, `toJSON()`, `sendPasswordReset()` and `calculateLoyaltyTier()`. Marketing keeps changing the tier rules, and those PRs collide with the auth team's edits to the same file. Which refactor follows the single responsibility principle?
choices: Make `calculateLoyaltyTier` a static method on `User`
Move the tier rules into their own `LoyaltyPolicy`
Split `User` into `UserBase` and `UserExtended` subclasses
Add an `IUser` interface listing every method of `User`
variants.explain: The tier rules have their own reason to change, so they get their own module, and the auth code stops changing with them. A static method or a subclass split keeps the rules in the same class hierarchy, still coupled to `User`.

concepts.title: Liskov substitution principle
concepts.summary: A subtype must keep the promises of the type it replaces, not just its method signatures

choices: Interface segregation
Dependency inversion
Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
variants.explain: Callers of `FileStore` rely on `save` working; a subtype that throws instead can't be substituted for its parent. Splitting the interface (interface segregation) is one possible fix, but the broken rule is substitutability.

choices: Interface segregation: the interface has too many methods
Nothing wrong: Go interfaces only promise method signatures
Dependency inversion: callers depend on a concrete type
Liskov substitution: it breaks the documented contract
variants.explain: Substitutability covers behaviour, not just types: an implementation that ignores the documented contract breaks every caller that relies on it. The compiler only checks signatures, which is exactly why the contract matters.

choices: Liskov substitution
Interface segregation
Open/closed
Single responsibility
variants.explain: `Square` narrows what `set_size` accepts, so code written against `Rectangle` fails with valid input. A subtype may accept more than its parent, never less.

variants.q: A base class method `parse(input)` accepts any string and returns a result, or an empty result for garbage. Which override in a subclass is safe for code written against the base class?
choices: Rejecting inputs longer than 1000 characters with an exception
Returning `null` instead of an empty result for garbage
Also accepting `null` and returning an empty result for it
Requiring callers to run `init()` before the first `parse`
variants.explain: A subtype may accept more than its parent and promise at least as much, never the reverse. Rejecting inputs, returning `null` or adding a setup step all break callers that were correct against the base class.

concepts.title: Dependency inversion principle
concepts.summary: High-level code depends on an abstraction it owns; the concrete detail is plugged in from outside

variants.q: Package `orders` needs to save orders, and package `postgres` implements storage. Following dependency inversion and Go convention, where does the `OrderStore` interface usually live?
choices: In `postgres`, next to the implementation
In `orders`, the package that uses it
In a shared `interfaces` package both import
Nowhere: `orders` imports `postgres` directly
variants.explain: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so the convention is that the consumer defines the small interface it needs. Then `orders` never imports `postgres`; the detail depends on the policy. A shared interfaces package works but couples every package to it for no gain.

choices: Read `SMTP_URL` from a config file instead of the environment
Make `mailer` public so tests can overwrite it after construction
Take a `Mailer` in the constructor; wire `SmtpMailer` outside
Move `SmtpMailer` into the same file as `SignupService`
variants.explain: Injecting an abstraction means the service no longer knows which mailer it gets, so tests pass a fake and production passes `SmtpMailer`. Overwriting a public field works by accident: the real mailer is still constructed, and the dependency is still hard-coded.

choices: Monkeypatch `os.environ` in the tests so the URL is empty
Make `mailer` a class attribute so tests can replace it
Move `SmtpMailer` into the same module as `SignupService`
Accept a `Mailer` protocol in `__init__`
variants.explain: With the mailer passed in, the service depends only on the `Mailer` shape, and tests hand it a fake. An empty URL still builds the real client; a class attribute is still a hard-coded concrete dependency.

variants.q: Arrows mean 'imports'. Which dependency graph shows dependency inversion at work?
choices: `OrderService → PaymentPort ← StripePayment`
`OrderService → StripePayment → PaymentPort`
`OrderService → StripePayment → Stripe SDK`
`OrderService → PaymentPort → StripePayment`
variants.explain: The business code owns the abstraction and the detail points at it, so the source dependency runs against the call direction. In the other graphs the high-level code still reaches the concrete detail, directly or through an interface that depends on it.

concepts.title: Fragile base class
concepts.summary: A subclass breaks because it depends on how its parent calls its own methods internally

choices: `NaN`
variants.explain: `Bag.addAll` calls `this.add`, which dispatches to the override, so each item is counted twice. The subclass silently depends on the parent's internal self-calls; wrapping a `Bag` (composition) instead of extending it avoids that.

variants.q: `CountingBag` overrides only `add` (incrementing `count`) and relies on `Bag.add_all` calling `self.add` for each item. The `Bag` maintainers later change `add_all` to `self.items.extend(xs)`. No public signature changed. What happens to `CountingBag`?
choices: Python raises `TypeError` when `add_all` is called
`count` silently stops counting items added via `add_all`
`add_all` now calls `CountingBag.add` twice per item
Nothing: overridden methods are always called by the parent
variants.explain: The subclass depended on an implementation detail of its parent. A harmless-looking optimisation in the base class broke it with no error, which is why composition is usually safer than inheriting from classes you don't control.

variants.q: You subclass a library's `HttpClient` and override `get()` to add logging. A later release changes `getJson()` to call an internal `fetch()` instead of `get()`, and your logs for JSON calls vanish. No signature changed. What's the underlying problem, and the usual fix?
choices: You should also have overridden `getJson()`; always override every method
The library broke its versioning contract; only its maintainers can fix it
Logging belongs in a subclass of `fetch()`, not of `get()`
The subclass relied on the parent's internals; wrap the client instead
variants.explain: Inheriting from a class you don't control ties you to how it calls itself, and that can change without any visible API change. Composition (a wrapper that holds the client) only depends on the public methods.

variants.q: You want a vendor's `Cache` class's behaviour plus hit/miss metrics, and the vendor ships new versions often. Which approach is least likely to break on an upgrade?
choices: Subclass it and override only the method you care about
Subclass it and override every public method
Patch its methods at startup so existing callers pick up the metrics
Hold a `Cache` inside your own class and delegate to its public methods
variants.explain: Delegation depends only on the public contract, while a subclass also depends on which methods the parent calls on itself, and that can change between releases. Overriding every method still inherits those internal call paths.

concepts.title: Struct embedding is not inheritance
concepts.summary: Go promotes an embedded type's methods, but there is no virtual dispatch back to the outer type

choices: `hello child`
It doesn't compile: `Name` is ambiguous
`hello base`
It panics at runtime
variants.explain: `Child{}.Hello()` is shorthand for `Child{}.Base.Hello()`, and inside it the receiver is a `Base`, so `b.Name()` calls `Base.Name`. Embedding gives promotion, not overriding; to let the outer type customise behaviour, pass in an interface or a function.

choices: It doesn't compile: `prefix` is defined twice
`[base] hi`
variants.explain: `Log` is promoted from `Logger` and runs with a `Logger` receiver, which knows nothing about `ReqLogger.prefix`. The outer method only wins when called on the outer value directly.

concepts.title: Law of Demeter
concepts.summary: Talk to your direct collaborators, not to objects reached through them

variants.q: `invoice.getCustomer().getAccount().getBillingAddress().getCountry()` appears in 30 places. Billing addresses move from `Account` to `Customer`, and all 30 call sites break. Which guideline would have limited the damage?
choices: Law of Demeter
Liskov substitution principle
Interface segregation principle
Command-query separation
variants.explain: Each caller depended on the internal structure of three objects it was never given. Asking `invoice.billingCountry()` would have kept that knowledge in one place.

variants.q: A `checkout(order)` method makes these calls. Which one breaks the Law of Demeter?
choices: `order.total()`
`order.customer().wallet().debit(amount)`
`this.payments.charge(order.total())`
`this.logger.info('checkout', { id: order.id })`
variants.explain: Reaching through the customer into its wallet, then changing the wallet, couples checkout to the structure of two objects it wasn't handed. The others call methods on a parameter or on the method's own fields.

concepts.title: DRY (don't repeat yourself)
concepts.summary: Each piece of knowledge, such as a business rule, lives in one authoritative place

variants.q: The rule 'orders over $100 ship free' is written as `if total > 100` in the checkout service, the cart page and the confirmation email. Marketing lowers it to $75, and only two of the three places get updated. Which principle was broken?
choices: Liskov substitution
Don't repeat yourself (DRY)
Interface segregation
Law of Demeter
variants.explain: DRY says each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation; the threshold was one business rule copied into three places, so a change had to find every copy. Liskov substitution is about subtypes keeping their parent's promises, which isn't involved here.

variants.q: Two modules each contain the same three validation lines today: one checks shipping addresses, the other billing addresses. Different teams own the two rules, and they're expected to diverge. A reviewer says DRY requires one shared helper. What does DRY actually ask for?
choices: One helper, since any repeated code breaks DRY
One helper with a flag parameter for each caller
A shared base class that both modules inherit
One home per piece of knowledge, so these can stay apart
variants.explain: DRY is about duplicated knowledge, not code that happens to look alike. Two rules that change for different reasons are separate knowledge, and merging them would couple changes that should stay independent.

skills.title: Design patterns
skills.summary: Common patterns like strategy, adapter and decorator, and when they fit

concepts.title: Strategy pattern
concepts.summary: Swapping one algorithm for another behind a shared interface, chosen at runtime

variants.q: A `price()` function has a `switch` on customer type (`retail`, `wholesale`, `staff`), and every new pricing rule adds a case. You want each rule in its own object, chosen at runtime, behind one interface. Which pattern is that?
choices: Observer
Decorator
Strategy
Singleton
variants.explain: Strategy puts each interchangeable algorithm behind one interface and lets the caller pick one. Decorator also shares an interface, but it wraps another object to add behaviour rather than replacing the algorithm.

choices: Adapter
Template method
Facade
Strategy
variants.explain: The caller passes in the algorithm, and `Upload` works with any of them through one interface. Template method would fix the steps in a base type and let subclasses fill some in, which isn't what happens here.

variants.q: `items.sort(byPrice)` and `items.sort(byDate)`: `sort` is written once, and the caller passes in the comparison rule. Which pattern fits best?
choices: Decorator
Strategy
Observer
Adapter
variants.explain: The comparison is one interchangeable algorithm the caller selects, with the rest of the routine unchanged. A decorator would wrap `sort` to add behaviour around it rather than swap a step inside.

concepts.title: Decorator (wrapper) order
concepts.summary: Wrapping something in a layer with the same interface to add behaviour; the outer layer runs first

choices: `Logging`, then `Auth`, then `api`
`Auth`, then `Logging`, then `api`
`api`, then `Auth`, then `Logging`
Not defined: middleware runs concurrently
variants.explain: Each middleware is a decorator around the handler it receives. The outermost wrapper sees the request first, so `Logging` runs before `Auth` even though `Auth` was applied first.

variants.q:
`withRetry` tries `fn` up to 3 times; `withTimeout` rejects if `fn` takes longer than `ms`. What does the 1000 ms bound here?

```ts
const call = withRetry(withTimeout(fetchUser, 1000))
```
choices: All attempts together, so the whole call never takes over 1 s
Each attempt on its own, up to about 3 s in all
Only the first attempt; retries run without a timeout
Nothing: the outer wrapper replaces the inner one
variants.explain: The timeout wraps `fetchUser`, and the retry wraps that, so every attempt gets its own 1 s. To bound the total, swap the order: `withTimeout(withRetry(fetchUser), 1000)`.

choices: All attempts together, so the whole call never takes over 1 s
Only the first attempt; retries run without a timeout
Each attempt on its own, up to about 3 s in all
Nothing: only the top decorator takes effect
variants.explain: Decorators apply bottom-up, so this is `with_retry(with_timeout(fetch_user))`: each attempt is timed separately. Put `with_timeout` on top to bound the whole call.

variants.q: `const store = cached(audited(rawStore))`. Each wrapper implements the same `Store` interface; `audited` logs every read it sees, and `cached` answers a hit without calling the store it wraps. A read hits the cache. Is it audited?
choices: Yes: `audited` was applied first, so it runs first
No: `cached` answers before the call reaches `audited`
Yes: every wrapper in the chain runs on every call
No: wrappers audit writes only, never reads
variants.explain: The outermost wrapper sees the call first and can stop it, so an inner layer is skipped on a cache hit. To audit every read, put `audited` on the outside: `audited(cached(rawStore))`.

concepts.title: Adapter pattern
concepts.summary: A thin wrapper that makes an existing interface look like the one your code expects

variants.q: Your code depends on a `Notifier` interface with `send(userId, text)`. A vendor SDK you're adopting exposes `postMessage({ recipient, body, channel })`. You write a small class that implements `Notifier` by calling the SDK. Which pattern is that?
choices: Facade
Bridge
Observer
Adapter
variants.explain: An adapter converts one interface into another that callers already expect. A facade offers a new, simpler interface over a complex subsystem; here the target interface already existed.

variants.q: The standard library's `http.HandlerFunc` type lets an ordinary `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)` be used anywhere an `http.Handler` is required. Which pattern is that?
choices: Adapter
Decorator
Strategy
Factory method
variants.explain: `HandlerFunc` gives a plain function the `ServeHTTP` method the `Handler` interface needs, converting one shape into another; Go's own docs call it an adapter. It adds no behaviour, so it isn't a decorator.

variants.q: Your code defines a `Storage` interface. Which of these is an adapter?
choices: A class implementing `Storage` that adds retries around another `Storage`
A `Checkout` class calling payments, shipping and email in one method
A class implementing `Storage` by calling a vendor's S3 SDK
A function that picks a `Storage` implementation from an env variable
variants.explain: An adapter translates an existing interface into the one your code expects. The retry wrapper is a decorator, the checkout class is a facade, and the picker is a factory.

concepts.title: Functional options
concepts.summary: Go pattern: configure a constructor with variadic `func(*T)` options over defaults

choices: It panics: an option was set twice
variants.explain: Options run in order over the defaults, so the last `WithPort` wins and the untouched timeout keeps its default.

variants.q: What's the main advantage of `NewServer(opts ...Option)` over `NewServer(port int, timeout time.Duration, tls *tls.Config)`?
choices: The compiler checks that every required setting was passed
Options are applied concurrently, so construction is faster
New settings can be added without breaking callers
The returned `*Server` can no longer be modified afterwards
variants.explain: Adding a `WithX` function doesn't change the constructor's signature, and callers only mention what they change. The flip side: nothing forces a caller to pass a required setting, so required values are better as plain parameters.

concepts.title: EventEmitter is synchronous
concepts.summary: Node's `emit` calls every listener immediately, in order, before it returns

variants.q:
What's logged?

```ts
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events'

const e = new EventEmitter()
e.on('order', () => console.log('A'))
e.emit('order')
console.log('B')
```
choices: `B` then `A`
Only `B`
The order varies between runs
`A` then `B`
variants.explain: `emit` runs listeners synchronously, so `A` is logged before `emit` returns. It isn't queued like a promise callback or `setTimeout`.

variants.q: Three listeners are registered for `'order'` on a Node `EventEmitter`. The second throws synchronously. What happens on `emit('order')`?
choices: It throws out of `emit`; the third listener doesn't run
The error is logged and the third listener still runs
The error is re-emitted as an `'error'` event instead
`emit` returns `false` and nothing is thrown
variants.explain: Listeners are plain synchronous calls inside `emit`, so a throw unwinds straight to the caller and skips the rest. `EventEmitter` doesn't turn a listener's synchronous throw into an `'error'` event.

concepts.title: Wrappers hide optional interfaces
concepts.summary: In Go, wrapping a value in your own struct drops the extra interfaces the original implemented, like `http.Flusher`

choices: Type assertions fail on any struct that embeds an interface
The field's static type is `ResponseWriter`, so `Flush` isn't promoted
The assertion only succeeds after `WriteHeader` has run
Only HTTP/2 connections implement `http.Flusher`
variants.explain: Embedding promotes the method set of the field's declared type, and `http.ResponseWriter` has no `Flush`, even though the value inside does. Assertions on structs that embed interfaces work fine for the methods that are promoted. Fix it by forwarding `Flush` yourself, or with an `Unwrap` method and `http.ResponseController`.

variants.q: Since Go 1.20, what lets `http.NewResponseController(w).Flush()` reach the real writer through a wrapper like `statusRecorder`, without the wrapper defining `Flush` itself?
choices: A `Hijack()` method that returns the raw connection
Registering the wrapper with `http.RegisterWrapper`
An `Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter` method on the wrapper
Embedding `*http.response` instead of the interface
variants.explain: `ResponseController` checks the writer for the method it needs and, if it's missing, follows `Unwrap()` to the wrapped writer. `http.RegisterWrapper` doesn't exist, and `*http.response` is unexported, so other packages can't embed it.

skills.title: API design
skills.summary: Clear, consistent APIs: naming, errors, pagination and versioning

concepts.title: Idempotency keys
concepts.summary: A client-chosen key that lets the server recognise a retried request and replay its first result

variants.q: A mobile client sends `POST /payments`. The server charges the card, but the response is lost to a timeout, and the client retries. Which design stops the retry from charging twice?
choices: The server rejects any second payment from that same user for 60 seconds
The client sends an `Idempotency-Key`; the server replays the result
The client retries with `PUT /payments`, because PUT is idempotent
The server wraps the charge in a transaction so it can roll back
variants.explain: The key ties the retry to the first attempt, so the server returns the saved outcome instead of charging again. Switching to PUT changes the label, not the server's behaviour, and a database rollback can't undo a card charge.

variants.q: Your API supports `Idempotency-Key`. A client retries with the same key but a different `amount` in the body. What's the safest response?
choices: Replay the stored response from the first request
Process it as a new payment, since the body changed
Reject it: the key belongs to a different request
Update the first payment to the new amount
variants.explain: A reused key with a different payload is a client bug; silently replaying or processing it would hide that. Replaying is right only when the request matches the original.

concepts.title: Cursor (keyset) pagination
concepts.summary: Paging by 'rows after this one' instead of by offset, so inserts don't shift pages

variants.q: A feed uses `?offset=20&limit=20`, newest first. While a user reads page 1, five new posts are published. What does page 2 show?
choices: Exactly the next 20 posts with no overlap
Only the five newly published posts
An error, because the total count changed
Five posts from page 1 again
variants.explain: The offset counts from the top, and the five new posts pushed everything down. A cursor such as `?after=<last id>` anchors the page to a row, so new posts don't shift it.

variants.q: You page by `created_at DESC`, and the cursor holds the last row's `created_at`. Why should it also hold the row's `id`, ordering by `(created_at, id)`?
choices: Rows sharing a timestamp get skipped or repeated
Ids sort faster than timestamps in every database engine
Clients need the id to fetch the full row afterwards
A cursor without the `id` can't be signed against tampering
variants.explain: If several rows share the boundary timestamp, `<` skips the unseen ones and `<=` repeats the seen ones. A unique tie-breaker makes the position exact.

concepts.title: Backward-compatible API changes
concepts.summary: Which changes existing clients survive, and which ones break them

variants.q: Which change to a public JSON API response is backward compatible for well-behaved clients?
choices: Renaming `user_id` to `userId`
Adding a new optional field
Changing `price` from a number to a string
Removing a field the docs mark as deprecated
variants.explain: Clients that ignore unknown fields are unaffected by an addition. Removing a field breaks anyone still reading it, deprecation notice or not.

variants.q: You delete `string coupon = 7;` from a protobuf message that older clients still send and read. What should you add?
choices: Nothing: protobuf ignores missing fields anyway
A new field 7 with the same name and a new type
`reserved 7;`, so the number can't be reused later
`optional` on every remaining field in the message
variants.explain: Old clients still put data under number 7. If a later field reuses it with a different meaning, they'll be misread; reserving the number (and name) prevents that. Deleting alone is safe today but leaves that trap.

concepts.title: 202 Accepted for long-running work
concepts.summary: Accepting a slow job right away and giving the client a status resource to check

variants.q: `POST /backups` starts a database snapshot that takes several minutes. What's the usual response?
choices: `200 OK` after holding the request open until it finishes
`201 Created` with the finished backup in the body
`504 Gateway Timeout`, so the client retries later
`202 Accepted` and a URL for a status resource to poll
variants.explain: 202 says the work was accepted but isn't done, and the status URL lets the client follow it. Holding the connection open for minutes runs into proxy and client timeouts.

variants.q: A client gets `202 Accepted` with `Location: /operations/7f3a` from `POST /videos/9/transcode`. What does the 202 tell it?
choices: It was accepted but isn't done, and may still fail
The transcode is finished and the result is at `/operations/7f3a`
The server guarantees the work will finish successfully
The server was too busy to validate it and will retry
variants.explain: 202 promises nothing about the outcome, only that processing will happen later. The client learns the result from the status resource.

concepts.title: Spec-first API design (OpenAPI)
concepts.summary: Writing and reviewing the OpenAPI spec before the code, then generating clients or validators from it

concepts.title: Consistent error responses
concepts.summary: Failures use the right HTTP status plus one stable, machine-readable error body across the API

variants.q: When a payment fails, an API returns `200 OK` with `{"ok": false, "error": "card declined"}`. What's the main problem?
choices: Clients, proxies and monitors all see it as a success
Error responses aren't allowed to carry a JSON body
Browsers will cache the failed response indefinitely
Clients can't reliably parse a boolean error flag
variants.explain: Everything that looks at the status line (HTTP clients, retries, gateways, dashboards, alerts) counts this as a success. A 4xx status with an error body tells both machines and people that it failed.

variants.q: A mobile app must show one screen when a coupon has expired and a different one when the coupon doesn't exist. Which error design supports that best?
choices: Return 400 and let the app match on the message text
Return 422 with an empty body and document the meaning
Return 500 so the app retries until the coupon works
Return 400 with a stable `code` such as `coupon_expired`
variants.explain: A stable code is a contract clients can branch on, while the message stays free to change and be translated. Matching on message text breaks the first time someone rewords it.

concepts.title: Hyrum's law
concepts.summary: With enough users, every observable behaviour of an API gets depended on, whatever the docs promise

variants.q: Your API docs say list results come back 'in no particular order'. For years they happened to be sorted by id. You're about to move to a new store that returns them unsorted, and the API has thousands of integrators. How should you treat the change?
choices: As safe, since the order was never documented
As safe for clients that use the official SDK
As breaking: assume someone relies on the id order
As breaking only if the response schema changes too
variants.explain: Hyrum's law: with enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by someone, whatever the docs say. You may still ship it, but announce it or keep the sort, rather than assume nobody notices.

variants.q: You want to reword an error message from 'User not found' to 'No such user'. The docs say only the `code` field is stable. With many clients, what's the realistic expectation?
choices: No client can break, since the message is undocumented
Only clients on an older API version can be affected
Clients break only if the HTTP status changes too
Some clients likely match on the text and may break
variants.explain: Documentation doesn't stop people depending on what they can observe, so at scale even message text becomes part of the de facto contract. You may still decide to change it, but expect breakage and announce it.

skills.title: System design
skills.summary: Designing whole systems for scale and failure, and weighing trade-offs

concepts.title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
concepts.summary: Scaling up to a bigger machine vs scaling out to more instances, which works best when instances are stateless

variants.q: A web service keeps each user's shopping cart in an in-memory map. The team adds two more instances behind a round-robin load balancer, and users report carts that empty and refill at random. Which fix lets the service keep scaling out?
choices: Move the service to one bigger machine instead
Keep cart state in a shared store such as Redis
Shorten the load balancer's health-check interval
Send each request to all three instances at once
variants.explain: Each instance has its own memory, so consecutive requests from one user land on instances holding different carts. Moving state to a shared store makes instances interchangeable; one bigger machine works too, but that's scaling up, with a hardware ceiling and a single point of failure.

variants.q: A single API server is at 90% CPU. The team can move it to a machine with twice the cores (vertical scaling) or run several copies behind a load balancer (horizontal scaling). What's true of the vertical option?
choices: Usually no code changes, but capped by the largest machine
It removes the single point of failure of one server
It always costs less per unit of capacity than adding servers
It only works once the service has become stateless
variants.explain: Scaling up keeps the same single process, so code rarely changes, but there's a largest machine you can buy and it's still one point of failure. Statelessness is what horizontal scaling needs, not vertical.

concepts.title: Cascading failure
concepts.summary: One slow or failing service exhausts its callers' resources, and the failure spreads upstream

variants.q: Service A calls B with no timeout. B's database slows down, B's answers take over a minute, and soon A runs out of threads and connections and fails health checks, even for requests that don't need B. What is this called?
choices: Thundering herd
Cascading failure
Split brain
Head-of-line blocking
variants.explain: B's slowness consumed A's resources until A failed too, and A's callers are next. A thundering herd is many clients waking at once for one resource, which is a different trigger.

variants.q: Which change most directly stops a slow dependency from taking its callers down with it?
choices: More read replicas for the dependency's database
Longer timeouts so slow calls get time to finish
Short timeouts plus a circuit breaker
Retrying failed calls immediately, up to five times
variants.explain: Failing fast keeps the caller's threads and connections free; the breaker stops calling a dependency that's already struggling. Longer timeouts and immediate retries do the opposite: they tie up more resources.

concepts.title: Retry storm
concepts.summary: Retries at many layers, or in lockstep, multiply load on a struggling dependency and keep it down

variants.q: A request goes A → B → C → database. Each service makes up to 4 attempts at its downstream call. The database is down. How many database calls can one user request cause?
variants.explain: A makes 4 calls to B; each makes 4 to C (16); each of those makes 4 to the database (64). Retries multiply per layer, so retry at a single layer, or give each layer a retry budget.

variants.q: A dependency recovers from a short outage, then immediately falls over again under several times its normal traffic, over and over. Clients retry every failure at once, without limit. Which fix targets the cause?
choices: Cap retries with a budget and back off
Give every client call a longer timeout
Restart the dependency more often
Turn on HTTP keep-alive between clients and server
variants.explain: The extra load is the retries themselves, all landing as the service comes back. Limiting how many retries are allowed and spacing them out lets it recover.

choices: The shift overflows `time.Duration` within five attempts
They retry in lockstep; it needs random jitter
`<<` on a `time.Duration` doesn't compile in Go
`time.Sleep` pins the OS thread, starving other goroutines
variants.explain: Exponential delays alone keep clients synchronised: they all wake after 50 ms, then 100 ms, and hit the server together; random jitter spreads them out. The shift is legal because `Duration` is an integer type, and the delays only reach 800 ms.

variants.q: 5,000 clients lose their connection at the same instant and all retry with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...). Why add random jitter to each delay?
choices: Otherwise they all retry at the same instants, in synchronised waves
Random delays make each individual retry more likely to succeed
It lets the server tell which client is retrying each time
It keeps the delays from growing past the configured cap
variants.explain: Identical schedules keep clients in lockstep, so every wave lands at once. Jitter spreads the same retries over time; it doesn't make any single retry more likely to succeed.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: A slow consumer pushing back so the producer slows down, instead of a buffer growing without limit

choices: It blocks on `jobs <- j` until there is room
The oldest job in the channel is dropped
The send panics because the channel is full
The channel grows its buffer automatically
variants.explain: A blocking send on a full bounded channel is backpressure: the producer runs at the consumers' pace instead of piling up memory. Use `select` with `default` if you'd rather shed load.

choices: Ignore it: the data is buffered, so nothing is lost
Wait for the stream's `'drain'` event before writing more
Call `write` again with the same data until it returns `true`
Call `out.end()` and open a fresh stream
variants.explain: `false` means the internal buffer is over its high-water mark. The data is kept, but if you keep writing, memory grows without limit; waiting for `'drain'` is how a stream applies backpressure (`pipeline` does it for you).

variants.q:
The consumers fall behind and the queue fills up. What happens to the producer?

```python
queue: asyncio.Queue[Job] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)

async def produce(incoming: list[Job]) -> None:
    for job in incoming:
        await queue.put(job)
```
choices: The oldest job in the queue is dropped
`put` raises `asyncio.QueueFull` right away
It waits at `await queue.put(job)`
The queue grows past `maxsize` automatically
variants.explain: On a bounded `asyncio.Queue`, `put` waits for space, so the producer slows to the consumers' pace. `put_nowait` is the one that raises `QueueFull`.

variants.q: A service accepts jobs into an unbounded in-memory queue. A downstream system is slower than the arrival rate, and hours later the process dies with out-of-memory. Which change adds backpressure?
choices: Bound the queue; make producers wait or get 'try later' when full
Raise the memory limit so the queue can hold more jobs
Write the queued jobs to a log file so they survive a restart
Retry each failed job immediately in a tight loop forever
variants.explain: The queue grew because nothing pushed back on producers; a bound turns overload into waiting or an explicit rejection. More memory or a durable log only delays the same problem.

concepts.title: Blast radius
concepts.summary: How much of the system, or how many users, one failure or bad change can affect

variants.q: All tenants share one worker pool. One tenant imports 2 million rows, and every other tenant's jobs wait an hour. Which change reduces the blast radius of one tenant's load?
choices: More workers in the shared pool
Strict first-in, first-out order across all tenants
An alert that fires when the queue gets long
A cap on how many workers one tenant can hold
variants.explain: Capping each tenant's share isolates them, so one tenant's spike only slows that tenant. More capacity in a shared pool just raises the size of spike needed to hit everyone, and strict FIFO is what let the import take every worker.

variants.q: A config change will go to all five regions. Which rollout limits the blast radius if the change turns out to be bad?
choices: One region first, check its metrics, then the rest in stages
All regions at once, with a tested rollback script ready to run
All regions at once, in the quietest hour of the day
The largest region first, since it has the best monitoring
variants.explain: A staged rollout caps how much breaks before you notice. A rollback script helps you recover, but every region is already affected by then.

concepts.title: Circuit breaker
concepts.summary: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then lets a few trial calls through

variants.q: A circuit breaker on calls to a payment provider is **open**. What happens to a new call?
choices: It's queued until the provider recovers
It fails immediately
It's sent with a doubled timeout
It's sent, and the response is ignored
variants.explain: Open means 'stop trying': calls fail fast, which protects both your resources and the struggling provider. Queueing would just move the pile-up somewhere else.

variants.q: After its open period ends, a breaker goes **half-open**. What does it do in that state?
choices: Sends half of all calls through and fails the other half
Retries the last failed call in a loop until it works
Lets a few trial calls through to test recovery
Waits for an operator to reset it by hand
variants.explain: Half-open is a probe: a small number of calls test whether the dependency has recovered before full traffic returns.

concepts.title: Upstream/downstream contracts
concepts.summary: What a service promises the services that depend on it, and how to change it without breaking them

variants.q: Your service publishes `order.created` with `amount` as an integer number of cents. Three teams consume it. You now need decimal amounts as strings. What's the safe change?
choices: Change `amount` to a string and announce it in the team channel
Keep the topic, add a `version` header, and change `amount` in place
Ask consumers to accept either format in `amount` from now on
Add `amount_decimal`, move consumers, then drop `amount`
variants.explain: Adding alongside, migrating, then removing keeps every consumer working at each step. Changing the field in place breaks anyone who misses the announcement or ignores the header.

variants.q: A consumer validates incoming events against a strict schema that rejects unknown properties. The producer adds a new optional field, and the consumer starts failing every message. Which practice would have avoided this?
choices: Consumers ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
Producers never add fields once a topic has consumers
Each consumer pins the producer's exact build version
The producer validates events against its own schema
variants.explain: Additive changes are only safe if consumers tolerate them. The producer's own schema check passes, since the new event is valid; freezing the producer or pinning builds makes the contract impossible to evolve.

concepts.title: Deadline propagation
concepts.summary: Passing the caller's remaining time budget down the call chain so nobody works past it

variants.q:
`parent` has 1 second left before its deadline. What is the deadline of `ctx`?

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
```
choices: 5 seconds from now
1 second from now: the parent's deadline
6 seconds from now
None: `WithTimeout` replaces the parent's deadline
variants.explain: A derived context can only shorten a deadline, never extend it. If the parent expires first, the child expires with it.

variants.q: A gateway gives up on requests after 3 s. Behind it, service A calls service B with its own fresh 10 s timeout, and no deadline or cancellation is passed along. B is slow today. What's the cost?
choices: The gateway raises its own timeout to 10 s to match
B's work is cancelled as soon as the gateway times out
A and B work for up to 10 s on answers nobody waits for
Nothing: the shortest timeout in the chain applies everywhere
variants.explain: Without a propagated deadline, each hop only knows its own timeout, so A and B burn capacity on answers nobody will receive. Under load that wasted work is what turns slowness into an outage.

variants.q: A request arrives at service A with 2 seconds left before the caller gives up. A spends 800 ms on its own work, then calls service B. Which timeout should it use for the call to B?
choices: A fresh 2 s, the original budget
About 1.2 s, or a little less
B's own default timeout, say 30 s
None: the caller already has a timeout
variants.explain: Only the remaining budget is still useful: an answer after the caller has left is wasted work. Passing it down (and leaving a margin for the way back) stops each hop from burning capacity on abandoned requests.

skills.title: Architecture decisions
skills.summary: Choosing between options, recording why (ADRs) and the trade-offs

concepts.title: Architecture decision record (ADR)
concepts.summary: Writing down a significant decision with its context, options and consequences, kept with the code

variants.q: Two years ago an ADR recorded the choice of RabbitMQ. The team is now moving to Kafka. What's the usual way to handle the old ADR?
choices: Edit it to say Kafka, so the record stays current
Delete it, since the decision no longer applies
Leave it and mention the move in the README
Write a new ADR for Kafka and mark the old one superseded
variants.explain: ADRs are an append-only log: the old one still explains why RabbitMQ made sense then, and the new one links to it. Editing or deleting it loses the history that ADRs exist to keep.

variants.q: Which of these is most worth an ADR?
choices: Renaming a private helper function in one package
Choosing Postgres over DynamoDB for orders
Fixing a typo in the team's onboarding guide
Bumping a library's patch version this week
variants.explain: ADRs are for significant decisions that are costly to reverse and that future engineers will ask 'why?' about. The others are small, reversible changes a commit message covers.

concepts.title: Distributed monolith
concepts.summary: Services that are separate on the network but still have to change and deploy together

variants.q: Your system has eight services. A feature usually needs four of them deployed together in a set order, and they all read and write the same database tables. What is this usually called?
choices: A modular monolith
A service mesh
An event-driven architecture
A distributed monolith
variants.explain: Every change still needs a coordinated release, and now each call can also fail over the network. A modular monolith keeps the boundaries inside one deployable and has no network hops between them.

variants.q: A team splits a modular monolith into services. Which outcome means they've built a distributed monolith?
choices: They still release together and share tables
Each service has its own database and deploys alone
Services talk over a queue instead of HTTP
Two of the services use different languages
variants.explain: The test is coupling: if changes still need coordinated releases and shared data, the split added network hops without independence. Transport and language don't decide it.

concepts.title: Conway's law
concepts.summary: Systems end up mirroring the communication structure of the teams that build them

variants.q: A company has a web team, a mobile team and a backend team. Without anyone planning it, the system grows a separate API layer owned by each client team. Which law predicts this?
choices: Hyrum's law
Conway's law
Gall's law
Brooks's law
variants.explain: The boundaries in the software followed the boundaries between teams. Hyrum's law is about users depending on any observable behaviour of an API.

variants.q: You want three independently deployable domain services, but today two teams share every module. What is the 'inverse Conway manoeuvre'?
choices: Design the services first, then let each team pick one it likes
Merge everyone into one team so there's no boundary to fight
Reshape the teams around the domains you want
Split the codebase first, then hire a team per new service
variants.explain: Because architecture tends to follow team structure, you change the team structure deliberately to get the architecture you want.

concepts.title: Saga
concepts.summary: Splitting a cross-service operation into local steps, and undoing finished steps with compensating actions if a later one fails

variants.q: A trip booking reserves a flight in one service, then a hotel room in another; each has its own database. The flight is reserved, then the hotel says it's full. What does a saga do?
choices: Rolls back both databases with a distributed transaction
Retries the hotel booking until a room is free
Leaves the flight for a nightly cleanup job
Runs a compensating action that cancels the flight
variants.explain: A saga has no global rollback; each finished step is undone by its own compensating action. A full hotel is an answer, not a transient error, so retrying won't help.

variants.q: A saga reserves stock in one service, then charges the card in another. Compared with one ACID transaction, what does it give up?
choices: Isolation: others can see stock held before the charge
Durability: a finished step can be lost in a crash
Local atomicity: each step can half-apply its writes
Convergence: the data can never be made consistent
variants.explain: Each step commits on its own, so other requests see intermediate state, such as stock held for an order whose card may yet be declined. Each local step is still an ordinary atomic, durable transaction.

concepts.title: Strangler fig pattern
concepts.summary: Replacing a legacy system piece by piece behind a router, instead of a big-bang rewrite

variants.q: You're replacing a legacy billing system. A proxy sends `/invoices` to the new service while everything else still goes to the old one, and more routes move over time. Which pattern is this?
choices: Blue-green deployment
Strangler fig
Branch by abstraction
Big-bang rewrite
variants.explain: The new system grows around the old one, route by route, until nothing is left to send to the legacy side. Branch by abstraction is the in-code cousin: an interface inside the codebase instead of a router in front.

variants.q: What makes the strangler fig pattern lower risk than a full rewrite?
choices: The new system reuses the legacy schema, so no data has to move
The whole cut-over happens in one weekend, with a rollback plan
Each slice is proven live while the old system runs the rest
The legacy code is deleted on day one, so only one system exists
variants.explain: Small slices go live early and can be routed back if they misbehave, so problems surface one piece at a time instead of all at once on cut-over day.

concepts.title: Monolith vs microservices
concepts.summary: What splitting into services buys (independent deploys and scaling) and what it costs (network failures, distributed data)

variants.q: A team splits its monolith into services. Which new cost do they take on that the monolith didn't have?
choices: Calls between parts can now time out or fail partway
Code can no longer be shared through libraries
Each service must use a different language
Unit tests can no longer run without a database
variants.explain: In-process function calls become network calls, which can be slow, fail, or succeed on one side only, and data spread across services loses single-database transactions. Sharing libraries and writing unit tests still work as before.

variants.q: Which situation is the strongest reason to move part of a monolith into its own service?
choices: The codebase has grown past 100,000 lines
A team wants to try a new web framework
The full test suite takes over ten minutes
Its own team must deploy and scale it separately
variants.explain: Services pay off when a part needs an independent deploy cycle, scaling profile or owning team. Size, slow tests or framework curiosity can be fixed inside a monolith, without taking on network and data-consistency costs.
